statements.quote: In the future, ethics and compassion will be the most crucial human qualities healers can possess, and our AI buddies can take care of the knowledge base.
statements.context: Opening line (sincere, before the parody begins) of a Dante Canto III parody about GenAI in clinical care. The author predicts a division of labor in future healthcare: human clinicians supply ethics and compassion while AI systems hold the knowledge base.
statements.note: General trend forecast, no date. Sincere framing line that precedes the satire.

statements.quote: Through me, you enter the future of knowledge.
statements.context: First line of the parody inscription over the fictional 'ShmepicAI' EHR portal, rewriting Dante's gate of hell. The AI proclaims itself the future of knowledge and the end of lies. Echoes the sincere opening line about AI taking over the knowledge base, but voiced by the fictional AI in a piece that mocks AI limits (stale answers, wrong math, token limits).
statements.note: Parody voice (fictional AI inscription). Logged for recall; the claim itself is satirical grandiosity.

statements.quote: Thus was the character count reached, and yet I realized I had many iterations yet to go before answers to my patients most crucial queries would be found.
statements.context: Closing line of the parody, narrator's voice (the author as clinician using GenAI in an EHR). After stale, wrong and truncated responses, he concludes that many more iterations of the technology are needed before AI answers patients' most crucial clinical questions. The underlying claim (GenAI is far from answering crucial clinical queries) reads as the author's sincere view.
statements.note: Borderline: fictional framing, vague horizon ('many iterations yet to go'). Implies answers eventually come, but not soon.

statements.quote: I humbly submit that if HHS covers brain stimulation treatment more broadly than it does medications, the problem will resolve more quickly.
statements.context: Closing argument of a post on HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s program to reduce antidepressant prescribing (reported by Ellen Barry in the NYT). The author argues antidepressant discontinuation raises suicide risk and that CMS/HHS should remove prior authorization and prior-medication-trial requirements for TMS and other neuromodulation. Conditional forecast: broader HHS coverage of brain stimulation than of medications leads to faster resolution of the overmedication problem.
statements.note: Conditional ('if HHS covers ... then'). The condition is a policy the author advocates; the outcome ('the problem will resolve more quickly') is loosely defined.

statements.quote: the links at the bottom of the article in The NY Times give us a tantalizing hint at what the future could look like—or what the present looks like, if you are a reader of this newsletter.
statements.context: The author says the NYT article on Kennedy's antidepressant plan omitted brain stimulation, then points to a linked NYT brain stimulation article as a hint of the future of non-drug depression care. He lists ProlivRx, Flow, TMS, DBS, SWIFT, SAINT, One-D, Prism, and companies Salma Health, Radial (his own), Beckley Clinical, Mindful Health Solutions as that present/future.
statements.note: Hedged, vague implied forecast that brain stimulation is the future of non-pharmacologic depression treatment. Mentions Radial (author's company).

statements.quote: This year, offered to throw me a party. I didn’t have the time. I’ll get to it next year.
statements.context: Birthday post (the author turned 40-odd on May 6). Someone (name stripped in the text) offered a birthday party this year; he declined for lack of time and says he will do it next year. Personal plan, half-joking.
statements.note: Personal plan, low forecast value; jokey tone ('How important could it be?'). Likely CONTROL.

statements.quote: But the executive order, which may soon open a legal pathway to ibogaine treatment in the United States, arrived one day too late to have offered him that hope.
statements.context: Op-ed co-authored by Owen Muir and Robert Glatter, M.D. about the April 18, 2026 presidential executive order 'Accelerating Medical Treatments for Serious Mental Illness', which directs FDA and DEA to build a Right to Try pathway for investigational psychedelics including ibogaine. Hedged forecast that the order may soon open a legal US pathway to ibogaine treatment, told around a patient's suicide attempt.
statements.note: Co-authored post (Muir and Glatter); author adopts the claim. The authors later stress the pathway 'does not yet exist'.

statements.quote: The research is there. The policy is moving. It needs to move fast enough to reach the millions of people who are still deciding if it is worth hanging on till tomorrow.
statements.context: Closing of the ibogaine op-ed. After calling on FDA and DEA to build the Right to Try pathway 'with alacrity', the authors assert that policy on psychedelic/ibogaine access is in motion and demand speed. Trend claim plus normative demand.
statements.note: Borderline: 'The policy is moving' is a present trend claim implying continued movement; 'It needs to move fast enough' is normative. Co-authored.

statements.quote: All of these tools are becoming a standard part of Brain Medicine care.
statements.context: Discussing Dr. Linda Carpenter's iTBS-for-ADHD trial (Brain Stimulation, 2026), which combined TMS with MRI guidance and concurrent EEG. The author says this supports his 'brain medicine is here' thesis (advanced in the newsletter and at Radial): TMS, MRI and EEG tools are becoming standard parts of brain medicine care.
statements.note: Trend claim (present progressive) that implies future standardization. Mentions Radial (author's company).

statements.quote: This kind of care, when it’s deployed as Dr. Carpenter does, will require multiple disciplines working together, and it will enabled by AI.
statements.context: Same passage on the brain medicine thesis: the author forecasts that multimodal brain medicine care (TMS plus MRI plus EEG, as in Carpenter's lab) will require multidisciplinary teams and will be enabled by AI.
statements.note: Compound claim: multidisciplinary teams and AI enablement. No date.

statements.quote: That suggests that the difference that Dr. Carpenter has detected is actually a very large one—anything you can see clearly in a small sample is more likely to be a big difference at scale, if it replicates.
statements.context: Interpreting the results of the 34-adolescent double-blind sham-controlled crossover trial of iTBS for ADHD (significant effects on parent-reported working memory, ADHD symptoms, anger, depression, anxiety). The author infers the effect is likely large at scale, conditional on replication.
statements.note: Conditional expectation about effect size at scale; partly statistical reasoning rather than a dated call.

statements.quote: They even added an additional open-label accelerated iTBS follow up after the study, and that seems to be plausible as a treatment approach as well
statements.context: The Carpenter/Kavanaugh paper included an open-label twice-daily iTBS (3600 pulses/day, 5 or 10 days) follow-up in previously enrolled adolescents with ADHD. The author judges accelerated iTBS plausible as a treatment approach for ADHD.
statements.note: Borderline: plausibility judgment about a treatment approach; implies future viability of accelerated iTBS for ADHD.

statements.quote: Given the rapidly growing literature on safety and efficacy of protocols that administer numerous iTBS sessions per day ... accelerated may iTBS will may show improved feasibility and comparable efficacy to traditional once per day iTBS for ADHD.
statements.context: Block quote from the Kavanaugh/Carpenter paper's discussion, reproduced by the author right after he calls the accelerated approach plausible. The paper forecasts that accelerated iTBS may show improved feasibility and comparable efficacy to once-daily iTBS for ADHD.
statements.note: Quoted third-party forecast (the paper's authors), endorsed softly by the author ('seems to be plausible'). Coder may set own_claim false.

statements.quote: We will, of course, need to replicate these findings, and more work will be done before there’s an FDA label from somebody. But it’s coming—obviously.
statements.context: After reviewing the third RCT showing TMS works in pediatric ADHD (first with brief iTBS at 80% threshold), the author forecasts that replication and more work are needed but an FDA label for TMS in ADHD from some company is coming. He then says payers need to hear the clamor as they have for accelerated TMS generally.
statements.note: Strong undated call: FDA label for TMS/iTBS in ADHD 'from somebody'. Compound with 'more work will be done' first.

statements.quote: a nationwide standard of medical necessity is being set in the treatment of depression, and it’s likely that PTSD, bipolar, depression, OCD, and even ADHD might be next.
statements.context: The author reports new accelerated TMS (SAINT and/or SWIFT) coverage policies in Blue Cross Blue Shield plans in California, Texas and South Carolina, following Highmark BCBS, Premera BCBS, CareFirst BCBS. He says a nationwide medical-necessity standard is being set for depression and forecasts PTSD, bipolar, OCD and ADHD coverage may follow.
statements.note: Compound: trend claim on depression coverage plus hedged forecast of expansion to other indications. SWIFT is the author's own protocol (BrainsWay).

statements.quote: It may be that the days of highly restrictive coverage policies, I’m looking at you other payors—might also need to be updated!
statements.context: Right after listing BCBS plans that now cover accelerated TMS, the author suggests that other payers' highly restrictive coverage policies may also need updating. Hedged, partly normative.
statements.confidence_phrase: It may be ... might also need to be updated
statements.note: Borderline: 'need to be updated' is normative; 'It may be that the days ... ' implies an expectation that restrictive policies end.
